## Setup

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)
```

If `palmerpenguins` is not installed yet, run `install.packages("palmerpenguins")` once, in the Console.

## The data {.smaller}

We use the `penguins` data set from the lecture: 344 penguins, 3 species, 3 islands.

```{r}
glimpse(penguins)
```

Some values are missing (`NA`). Keep that in mind: it matters for almost everything we do today.

---

## 1. Distributions

### 1.1 A normal distribution

`rnorm()` draws random numbers from a normal distribution. Draw 1000 values with a mean of 600 and a standard deviation of 80 (think of them as reaction times in ms), and save them into a tibble called `rt`.

Run `set.seed(1)` first: it makes sure we all get the **same** random numbers.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
```

::: solution

```{r}
rt <- tibble(value = rnorm(1000, mean = 600, sd = 80))
```

:::

### 1.2 Plot it

Plot the distribution of `value` with `geom_density()`.

::: solution

```{r}
ggplot(rt, aes(x = value)) +
  geom_density(fill = "plum2", alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "Reaction time (ms)", y = "Density")
```

:::

### 1.3 Change the spread

Draw another 1000 values with the **same** mean but `sd = 20`, and plot both distributions together. What changes, and what stays the same? Start with `set.seed(2)`.

```{r}
set.seed(2)
```

::: solution

```{r}
rt2 <- bind_rows(
  tibble(value = rnorm(1000, mean = 600, sd = 80), sd = "SD = 80"),
  tibble(value = rnorm(1000, mean = 600, sd = 20), sd = "SD = 20")
)
```

:::

::: solution

```{r}
ggplot(rt2, aes(x = value, fill = sd)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "Reaction time (ms)", y = "Density")
```

Both distributions are centred on 600 ms; the one with the smaller SD is much narrower.

:::

---

## 2. Central tendency

### 2.1 The mean

Compute the mean of `flipper_length_mm`. First try it directly: what happens?

::: solution

```{r}
mean(penguins$flipper_length_mm)
```

`NA` means "unknown". The mean of numbers that include an unknown value is unknown.

:::

There are two ways around it: remove the rows with missing values with `na.omit()` before taking the mean, or tell `mean()` to ignore them with `na.rm = TRUE`. Try both.

::: solution

```{r}
mean(na.omit(penguins)$flipper_length_mm)
mean(penguins$flipper_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE)
```

:::

The two numbers are **not** the same. Why? *Hint*: compare the number of rows.

::: {.solution .smaller}

```{r}
nrow(penguins)
nrow(na.omit(penguins))
sum(is.na(penguins$flipper_length_mm))
```

`na.omit()` removes every row with an `NA` in **any** column, including penguins whose flipper length we do know but whose `sex` is missing. `na.rm = TRUE` only ignores the `NA`s in the column we are summarising.

:::

### 2.2 The median

Compute the median of `flipper_length_mm`. Is it larger or smaller than the mean?

::: solution

```{r}
median(penguins$flipper_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE)
```

The median (`r median(penguins$flipper_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE)` mm) is smaller than the mean (`r round(mean(penguins$flipper_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE), 1)` mm).

:::

### 2.3 The mode

The mode is the most frequent value, and it is used with categorical data. Here is the function from the lecture:

```{r}
find_mode <- function(x) {
  u <- unique(x)
  tab <- tabulate(match(x, u))
  u[tab == max(tab)]
}
```

Which `island` do most penguins in the data come from? Which `species` is the most common?

::: solution

```{r}
find_mode(penguins$island)
find_mode(penguins$species)
```

:::

Check your answers with `count()`.

::: solution

```{r}
count(penguins, island)
count(penguins, species)
```

:::

---

## 3. Spread

### 3.1 Standard deviation, MAD and range

For `body_mass_g`, compute the standard deviation, the median absolute deviation, and the range.

::: solution

```{r}
sd(penguins$body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE)
mad(penguins$body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE)
range(penguins$body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE)
```

:::

How many grams separate the lightest and the heaviest penguin?

::: solution

```{r}
diff(range(penguins$body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE))
```

:::

### 3.2 Quantiles

`quantile()` gives the quartiles by default: the minimum, the 25%, 50% and 75% points, and the maximum. Compute them for `body_mass_g`. Which of these numbers is the median?

::: solution

```{r}
quantile(penguins$body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE)
```

The 50% point is the median: half of the penguins weigh less than `r median(penguins$body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE)` g.

:::

### 3.3 Outliers

Here are 10 reaction times from one participant:

```{r}
rts <- c(512, 548, 575, 590, 601, 615, 630, 644, 668, 702)
```

Compute the mean, the median, the SD and the MAD. Then add one very slow trial (the participant got distracted: 3000 ms) and compute them again. Which measures change a lot, and which barely move?

::: {.solution .smaller}

```{r}
c(mean = mean(rts), median = median(rts), sd = sd(rts), mad = mad(rts))

rts_slow <- c(rts, 3000)
c(mean = mean(rts_slow), median = median(rts_slow), sd = sd(rts_slow), mad = mad(rts_slow))
```

The mean and the SD are pulled up by a single trial. The median and the MAD are **robust**: they barely change.

:::

---

## 4. `group_by()` and `summarise()`

### 4.1 One group at a time

Compute the mean `body_mass_g` for each species, with `group_by()` and `summarise()`. Add the standard deviation and the number of penguins in each group, with `n()`.

::: solution

```{r}
penguins |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(mean_mass = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd_mass = sd(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE),
            n = n())
```

:::

### 4.2 The `.by` argument

Do the same with the `.by` argument instead of `group_by()`.

::: {.solution .smaller}

```{r}
penguins |>
  summarise(mean_mass = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd_mass = sd(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE),
            n = n(),
            .by = species)
```

The numbers are the same. Only the **order** of the rows may differ: `.by` keeps the groups in the order in which they first appear in the data.

:::

### 4.3 Bonus

Which island has the heaviest penguins on average? Sort the result from heaviest to lightest with `arrange(desc())`.

::: solution

```{r}
penguins |>
  summarise(mean_mass = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE), .by = island) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_mass))
```

:::

Is this a fair comparison between islands? *Hint*: run `count(penguins, island, species)`.

::: {.solution .smaller}

```{r}
count(penguins, island, species)
```

Only Biscoe has Gentoo penguins, the heaviest species. The difference between islands is mostly a difference between **species**.

:::
